claim: ADAR proteins alter gene expression by catalyzing adenosine (A) to inosine (I) RNA editing.
source: ADAR proteins alter gene expression both by catalyzing adenosine (A) to inosine (I) RNA editing and binding to regulatory elements in target RNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of ADAR proteins, representing established scientific knowledge about these proteins.

claim: ADAR proteins alter gene expression by binding to regulatory elements in target RNAs.
source: ADAR proteins alter gene expression both by catalyzing adenosine (A) to inosine (I) RNA editing and binding to regulatory elements in target RNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of ADAR proteins, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Loss of ADARs affects neuronal function in all animals studied to date.
source: Loss of ADARs affects neuronal function in all animals studied to date.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature throughout the manuscript and represents a synthesis of existing research.

claim: Caenorhabditis elegans lacking ADARs exhibit reduced chemotaxis.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans lacking ADARs exhibit reduced chemotaxis, but the targets responsible for this phenotype remain unknown.
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge from prior work (Tonkin et al., 2002) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: ADR-2 is the only A-to-I editing enzyme in C. elegans.
source: To identify critical neural ADAR targets in C. elegans, we performed an unbiased assessment of the effects of ADR-2, the only A-to-I editing enzyme in C. elegans, on the neural transcriptome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about C. elegans ADARs.

claim: SAILOR software identified 7361 A-to-I editing events across the neural transcriptome.
source: Development and implementation of publicly available software, SAILOR, identified 7361 A-to-I editing events across the neural transcriptome.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's computational analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: clec-41 is an edited mRNA whose neural expression is dependent on deamination.
source: Intersecting the neural editome with adr-2 associated gene expression changes, revealed an edited mRNA, clec-41, whose neural expression is dependent on deamination.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study combining editing site identification with differential expression analysis.

claim: Restoring clec-41 expression in adr-2 deficient neural cells rescued the chemotaxis defect.
source: Restoring clec-41 expression in adr-2 deficient neural cells rescued the chemotaxis defect, providing the first evidence that neuronal phenotypes of ADAR mutants can be caused by altered gene expression.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from transgenic rescue experiments.

claim: This study provides the first evidence that neuronal phenotypes of ADAR mutants can be caused by altered gene expression.
source: Restoring clec-41 expression in adr-2 deficient neural cells rescued the chemotaxis defect, providing the first evidence that neuronal phenotypes of ADAR mutants can be caused by altered gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing rescue of chemotaxis by clec-41 expression.

claim: ADARs convert adenosine (A) to inosine (I) within double-stranded RNA (dsRNA).
source: Adenosine deaminases that act on RNA (ADAR) are RBPs best known for converting adenosine (A) to inosine (I) within double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), including double-stranded regions of transcripts and small RNA precursors (Nishikura, 2010; Goodman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADAR function, supported by citations.

claim: RNA editing is prevalent in animal transcriptomes both in coding and non-coding regions of the genome.
source: Transcriptome-wide identification of A-to-I editing sites from a number of species has indicated that RNA editing is prevalent in animal transcriptomes both in coding and non-coding regions of the genome, but the genomic distribution of these editing sites vary in different organisms (Savva et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous transcriptome-wide studies.

claim: The genomic distribution of editing sites varies in different organisms.
source: Transcriptome-wide identification of A-to-I editing sites from a number of species has indicated that RNA editing is prevalent in animal transcriptomes both in coding and non-coding regions of the genome, but the genomic distribution of these editing sites vary in different organisms (Savva et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to comparative studies.

claim: Inosine is a biological mimic of guanosine.
source: As inosine is a biological mimic of guanosine, A-to-I editing has the potential to affect gene expression by altering coding potential, splice site selection, and/or small RNA binding (Deffit and Hundley, 2016; Nishikura, 2016; Tajaddod et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about inosine.

claim: A-to-I editing has the potential to affect gene expression by altering coding potential, splice site selection, and/or small RNA binding.
source: As inosine is a biological mimic of guanosine, A-to-I editing has the potential to affect gene expression by altering coding potential, splice site selection, and/or small RNA binding (Deffit and Hundley, 2016; Nishikura, 2016; Tajaddod et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles on ADAR function.

claim: Mammalian ADARs play editing-independent roles through binding to mRNAs and influencing the association of other RBPs on the same target RNA.
source: In addition, recent studies have shown mammalian ADARs play editing-independent roles through binding to mRNAs and influencing the association of other RBPs on the same target RNA (Anantharaman et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2013; Bahn et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies on mammalian ADARs.

claim: One of the primary biological functions of ADARs is to promote proper neuronal function.
source: One of the primary biological functions of ADARs is to promote proper neuronal function (Li and Church, 2013; Behm and Öhman, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The mammalian brain contains the highest level of inosine.
source: The mammalian brain contains the highest level of inosine, and A-to-I editing within coding regions of specific human transcripts, such as ion channels and receptors, alters the physiological properties of the encoded proteins, a requisite for proper neuronal function (Paul and Bass, 1998; Tariq and Jantsch, 2012; Rosenthal and Seeburg, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies measuring inosine levels.

claim: A-to-I editing within coding regions of specific human transcripts, such as ion channels and receptors, alters the physiological properties of the encoded proteins.
source: The mammalian brain contains the highest level of inosine, and A-to-I editing within coding regions of specific human transcripts, such as ion channels and receptors, alters the physiological properties of the encoded proteins, a requisite for proper neuronal function (Paul and Bass, 1998; Tariq and Jantsch, 2012; Rosenthal and Seeburg, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on recoding editing in mammalian neurons.

claim: Alterations in ADAR protein levels and editing activity have been observed in human neuropathological diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and many cancers, including brain tumors.
source: Consistent with this important role of ADARs in the mammalian nervous system, alterations in ADAR protein levels and editing activity have been observed in human neuropathological diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and many cancers, including brain tumors (Mannion et al., 2015; Bajad et al., 2017; Tomaselli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on ADARs in human disease.

claim: Mice lacking ADAR2 die of epileptic seizures by postnatal day 20 due to under-editing of one adenosine within the coding region of the glutamate receptor.
source: Mice lacking ADAR2 die of epileptic seizures by postnatal day 20 due to under-editing of one adenosine within the coding region of the glutamate receptor, which results in excessive calcium influx and neuronal excitoxicity (Higuchi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Higuchi et al. study.

claim: Under-editing of the glutamate receptor results in excessive calcium influx and neuronal excitotoxicity.
source: Mice lacking ADAR2 die of epileptic seizures by postnatal day 20 due to under-editing of one adenosine within the coding region of the glutamate receptor, which results in excessive calcium influx and neuronal excitoxicity (Higuchi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Higuchi et al. study.

claim: Loss of Drosophila melanogaster ADAR (dADAR) results in severe behavioral abnormalities, including extreme uncoordination, tremors, and a lack of courtship, as well as age-dependent neurodegeneration.
source: Loss of Drosophila melanogaster ADAR (dADAR) results in severe behavioral abnormalities, including extreme uncoordination, tremors, and a lack of courtship, as well as age-dependent neurodegeneration (Palladino et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Palladino et al. study.

claim: Loss of ADARs in C. elegans results in abnormal neuronal function as evidenced by defective chemotaxis to a number of volatile chemicals sensed by the AWA and AWC neurons.
source: Similar to the mouse and fly model organisms, loss of ADARs in C. elegans results in abnormal neuronal function as evidenced by defective chemotaxis to a number of volatile chemicals sensed by the AWA and AWC neurons (Tonkin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Tonkin et al. study.

claim: The chemotaxis defect in C. elegans ADAR mutants is less severe with increasing doses of volatile chemicals.
source: Loss of C. elegans ADARs likely affects the ability of the neurons to sense these chemicals as the chemotaxis defect is less severe with increasing doses of these volatiles (Tonkin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Tonkin et al. study.

claim: The targets responsible for the chemosensory defects of C. elegans ADARs were unknown prior to this study.
source: To date, the targets responsible for the chemosensory defects of C. elegans ADARs remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated as the knowledge gap that motivated the study.

claim: Previous studies using high-throughput sequencing to assess the editome and the role of ADR-2 have been limited to analyzing RNA isolated from whole worms.
source: Though multiple studies have used high-throughput sequencing to assess the editome and the role of ADR-2, these studies have been limited to analyzing RNA isolated from whole worms (Whipple et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2015; Goldstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous whole-worm studies.

claim: Chemomechanical disruption of worms followed by fluorescent activated cell sorting (FACS) can be used to obtain cells of interest from whole worms.
source: However, a recently developed method utilized chemomechanical disruption of worms followed by fluorescent activated cell sorting (FACS) to obtain cells of interest from whole worms (Spencer et al., 2014; Kaletsky et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the Spencer et al. and Kaletsky et al. studies.

claim: 22% of live cells were GFP positive in the FACS profile.
source: The FACS profile indicated that 22% of live cells were GFP positive, consistent with the proportion of neural cells in L1 worms (222/558) and similar to previously published studies using this technique (Figure 1B) (Spencer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a measurement from the FACS experiment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The proportion of GFP positive cells (22%) is consistent with the proportion of neural cells in L1 worms (222/558).
source: The FACS profile indicated that 22% of live cells were GFP positive, consistent with the proportion of neural cells in L1 worms (222/558) and similar to previously published studies using this technique (Figure 1B) (Spencer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the FACS data and known cell composition of L1 worms.

claim: The neural gene syntaxin (unc-64) is enriched in isolated neural cells compared to non-neural cells.
source: Consistent with neural enrichment in the GFP+ cells, qRT-PCR of a known neural gene, syntaxin (unc-64) (Saifee et al., 1998) indicated an enrichment in the isolated neural cells compared to non-neural cells (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The muscle gene myo-3 is depleted in isolated neural cells compared to non-neural cells.
source: whereas expression of the muscle gene, myo-3 (Ardizzi and Epstein, 1987), was depleted in the isolated neural cells compared to the non-neural cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only 28 editing events were identified in the adr-2(-) neural transcriptome.
source: This approach identified only 28 editing events in the adr-2(-) neural transcriptome, whereas 7377 events were identified in the wild-type neural transcriptome.
evidence: This is a result from the SAILOR analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: 7377 editing events were identified in the wild-type neural transcriptome.
source: This approach identified only 28 editing events in the adr-2(-) neural transcriptome, whereas 7377 events were identified in the wild-type neural transcriptome.
evidence: This is a result from the SAILOR analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: After subtracting sites identified in adr-2(-) neural transcriptome, 7361 A-to-I editing sites were predicted for the wild-type neural transcriptome.
source: After subtracting the sites that were identified in the adr-2(-) neural transcriptome, 7361 A-to-I editing sites were predicted for the wild-type neural transcriptome (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the SAILOR analysis after filtering.

claim: The 7361 predicted editing sites mapped to 549 genes.
source: The 7361 predicted editing sites mapped to 549 genes, 104 of which are novel edited targets (Supplementary file 1) (Goldstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a result from mapping editing sites to genes.

claim: 104 of the 549 edited genes are novel edited targets.
source: The 7361 predicted editing sites mapped to 549 genes, 104 of which are novel edited targets (Supplementary file 1) (Goldstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is determined by comparison with previously published edited targets.

claim: 86 of 86 predicted editing sites were confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
source: Importantly, 86 of 86 predicted editing sites (excluding 4 sites in which Sanger sequencing chromatogram had too much noise to accurately determine the presence of a true editing event) were confirmed (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is validation data from Sanger sequencing experiments.

claim: The false discovery rate (FDR) of SAILOR is less than 1%.
source: This data indicates the false discovery rate (FDR) of SAILOR is less than 1%, which is a significant improvement over the 6% FDR reported in our previously described algorithm (Washburn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the validation data showing 86/86 sites confirmed.

claim: SAILOR represents a significant improvement over the previously described algorithm which had a 6% FDR.
source: This data indicates the false discovery rate (FDR) of SAILOR is less than 1%, which is a significant improvement over the 6% FDR reported in our previously described algorithm (Washburn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with the previous algorithm cited.

claim: Sanger sequencing identified 87 additional editing sites in 7 genes beyond those called by SAILOR.
source: Furthermore, Sanger sequencing identified 87 additional editing sites in these 7 genes, demonstrating SAILOR can identify A-to-I editing sites on highly edited transcripts (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is validation data showing additional sites detected by Sanger sequencing.

claim: 92.4% of the 7361 editing sites were within genic regions when including 2000 base-pairs upstream and downstream annotations.
source: This analysis indicated that 92.4% of the 7361 editing sites were within genic regions, with the vast majority of these events occurring in the noncoding regions of protein-coding genes, including introns and UTRs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a result from the genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The vast majority of editing events occur in the noncoding regions of protein-coding genes, including introns and UTRs.
source: This analysis indicated that 92.4% of the 7361 editing sites were within genic regions, with the vast majority of these events occurring in the noncoding regions of protein-coding genes, including introns and UTRs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the genomic distribution analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: Only 83 editing sites (approximately 1%) were in coding regions.
source: Of the over 7300 events identified, only 83 editing sites (approximately 1%) were in coding regions.
evidence: This is a result from the genomic distribution analysis.

claim: The number of coding region editing sites is consistent with previous studies from whole-worms.
source: These data are consistent with the number of coding region editing sites previously identified from RNA isolated from whole-worms, and we identified nearly all of the same edited transcripts, including the heavily edited coding regions of histone genes (Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous whole-worm studies.

claim: Re-coding editing events are not enriched in the C. elegans nervous system.
source: Together, this data indicates that re-coding editing events are not enriched in the C. elegans nervous system and demonstrates that the role of C. elegans ADARs in the nervous system is not to generate proteomic diversity, but rather to fine-tune gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the low percentage of coding region editing sites.

claim: The role of C. elegans ADARs in the nervous system is not to generate proteomic diversity, but rather to fine-tune gene expression.
source: Together, this data indicates that re-coding editing events are not enriched in the C. elegans nervous system and demonstrates that the role of C. elegans ADARs in the nervous system is not to generate proteomic diversity, but rather to fine-tune gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the predominance of non-coding editing sites.

claim: 76 genes were ≥2 fold upregulated in neural cells lacking adr-2 compared to wild-type neural cells.
source: This analysis identified 76 genes that were ≥2 fold upregulated in neural cells lacking adr-2 as compared to wild-type neural cells and 93 genes that were ≥2 fold downregulated.
evidence: This is a result from the DESeq differential expression analysis.

claim: 93 genes were ≥2 fold downregulated in neural cells lacking adr-2 compared to wild-type neural cells.
source: This analysis identified 76 genes that were ≥2 fold upregulated in neural cells lacking adr-2 as compared to wild-type neural cells and 93 genes that were ≥2 fold downregulated.
evidence: This is a result from the DESeq differential expression analysis.

claim: Of the 169 differentially regulated genes, only four genes were identified as ADR-2 editing targets in neural cells.
source: Of these 169 differentially regulated genes, only four genes were identified as ADR-2 editing targets in neural cells, suggesting ADR-2 can also regulate expression of many genes via a mechanism that is independent of direct editing of the target mRNA.
evidence: This is a result from intersecting the editome with differentially expressed genes.

claim: ADR-2 can regulate expression of many genes via a mechanism that is independent of direct editing of the target mRNA.
source: Of these 169 differentially regulated genes, only four genes were identified as ADR-2 editing targets in neural cells, suggesting ADR-2 can also regulate expression of many genes via a mechanism that is independent of direct editing of the target mRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most differentially expressed genes are not edited.

claim: Loss of adr-2 regulates expression of genes at a tissue-specific level in C. elegans.
source: This reveals that loss of adr-2 regulates expression of genes at a tissue-specific level in C. elegans and suggests that these changes may not be observed in whole worm analysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that qRT-PCR of whole L1 larvae did not show the same expression changes as neural cells.

claim: Gene expression changes caused by loss of adr-2 may not be observed in whole worm analysis.
source: This reveals that loss of adr-2 regulates expression of genes at a tissue-specific level in C. elegans and suggests that these changes may not be observed in whole worm analysis.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing neural cell and whole worm qRT-PCR results.

claim: Editing sites were predicted in 82 genes that are associated with locomotion or chemotaxis GO terms.
source: Editing sites were predicted in 82 genes that are associated with locomotion or chemotaxis GO terms (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from GO term analysis of edited genes.

claim: Loss of adr-1 results in worms that are defective in sensing organic compounds, similar to loss of adr-2.
source: To narrow down this list of potential neurobiologically important targets, we focused on previous phenotypic data which demonstrated that, similar to the loss of adr-2, loss of adr-1 results in worms that are defective in sensing organic compounds (Tonkin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from the Tonkin et al. study.

claim: ADR-1 shares similar sequence and domain structure to ADR-2, though it lacks critical amino acids necessary for deamination.
source: ADR-1 shares similar sequence and domain structure to ADR-2, though it lacks critical amino acids necessary for deamination (Tonkin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from the Tonkin et al. study.

claim: ADR-1 promotes editing by ADR-2 at specific adenosines.
source: As ADR-1 promotes editing by ADR-2 at specific adenosines (Washburn et al., 2014), the similar phenotypes of adr-1(-) and adr-2(-) worms suggests that ADR-1 promotes editing by ADR-2 at sites important for proper chemotaxis.
evidence: This is cited from the Washburn et al. study.

claim: Of the 82 edited genes involved in locomotion/chemotaxis, 28 were identified as bound by ADR-1.
source: Of the 82 edited genes that are involved in proper worm locomotion/chemotaxis, 28 were identified as bound by ADR-1 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from intersecting edited genes with ADR-1 RIP-Seq data.

claim: Of the 28 genes bound by ADR-1, only clec-41 was also identified as differentially expressed in neural cells lacking adr-2.
source: Of these genes, only one, clec-41, was also identified as differentially expressed in neural cells lacking adr-2 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from intersecting multiple datasets.

claim: clec-41 mRNA shows >20 fold enrichment in ADR-1 immunoprecipitations from wild-type worms compared to those lacking adr-1.
source: Analysis of two independent biological replicates indicated a >20 fold enrichment of clec-41 mRNA in immunoprecipitations from wild-type worms compared to those lacking adr-1.
evidence: This is experimental data from ADR-1 RNA immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: clec-41 is a mRNA target of ADR-1.
source: Thus, consistent with the transcriptome-wide RIP-Seq, clec-41 is a mRNA target of ADR-1.
evidence: This is concluded from the RNA immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Wild-type neural cells exhibit A-to-I editing at 40 individual adenosines within the clec-41 3' UTR.
source: Consistent with clec-41 transcripts being bona fide targets of adenosine deamination, the wild-type neural cells exhibited A-to-I editing at 40 individual adenosines within the clec-41 3' UTR and this editing was absent in neural cells lacking adr-2 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is experimental data from Sanger sequencing shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Editing of clec-41 is absent in neural cells lacking adr-2.
source: Consistent with clec-41 transcripts being bona fide targets of adenosine deamination, the wild-type neural cells exhibited A-to-I editing at 40 individual adenosines within the clec-41 3' UTR and this editing was absent in neural cells lacking adr-2 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is experimental data from Sanger sequencing shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Editing of clec-41 is significantly altered at 12 sites in RNA isolated from adr-1(-) neural cells compared to wild-type neural cells.
source: Compared to RNA from wild-type neural cells, editing of clec-41 is significantly altered at 12 sites in RNA isolated from adr-1(-) neural cells (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is experimental data from Sanger sequencing shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ADR-1 regulation of editing at these adenosines was not observed in RNA isolated from L1 worms.
source: ADR-1 regulation of editing at these adenosines was not observed in RNA isolated from L1 worms (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is experimental data comparing neural cells to whole L1 worms shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only 2 of the 12 ADR-1 regulated editing sites exhibited similar editing levels between L1 and neural cell RNA.
source: In sum, only 2 of the 12 ADR-1 regulated editing sites exhibited similar editing levels between the L1 and neural cell RNA, suggesting neural-specific regulation of editing at these sites by ADR-1.
evidence: This is a comparison of editing data from neural cells and L1 worms.

claim: There is neural-specific regulation of editing at clec-41 sites by ADR-1.
source: In sum, only 2 of the 12 ADR-1 regulated editing sites exhibited similar editing levels between the L1 and neural cell RNA, suggesting neural-specific regulation of editing at these sites by ADR-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in editing patterns between neural cells and whole worms.

claim: Loss of adr-1 resulted in a three-fold reduction of clec-41 expression in neural cells.
source: Loss of adr-1 resulted in a three-fold reduction of clec-41 expression in neural cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Loss of adr-2 resulted in a three-fold downregulation of clec-41 expression in neural cells.
source: Consistent with the differential expression data, loss of adr-2 resulted in a similar three-fold downregulation and the regulatory effect of either adr-1 or adr-2 cannot be observed in RNA isolated from L1 worms (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The regulatory effect of either adr-1 or adr-2 on clec-41 expression cannot be observed in RNA isolated from L1 worms.
source: Consistent with the differential expression data, loss of adr-2 resulted in a similar three-fold downregulation and the regulatory effect of either adr-1 or adr-2 cannot be observed in RNA isolated from L1 worms (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is experimental data from qRT-PCR comparing neural cells to L1 worms shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Both ADR-1 and ADR-2 are required for proper clec-41 expression and editing in neural cells.
source: This suggests that both ADR-1 and ADR-2 are required for proper clec-41 expression and editing in neural cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression and editing data for both adr-1 and adr-2 mutants.

claim: Worms lacking either adr-1 or adr-2 and worms lacking both adr-1 and adr-2 have similar chemotaxis defects.
source: This is consistent with previous data that indicated a similar chemotaxis defect for worms lacking either adr-1 or adr-2 and worms lacking both adr-1 and adr-2 (Tonkin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from the Tonkin et al. study.

claim: This study is the first to identify an editing target whose expression is regulated by both C. elegans ADARs.
source: Despite the fact that the similarity in chemotaxis phenotypes has been known for over a decade, this study is the first to identify an editing target whose expression is regulated by both C. elegans ADARs.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: There is a need to assess editing and gene expression at a tissue-specific level in C. elegans.
source: Furthermore, this study brings into light the need to assess editing and gene expression at a tissue-specific level in C. elegans, as this molecular phenotype cannot be observed in RNA isolated from L1 worms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differences observed between neural cells and whole worms.

claim: clec-41 was previously found to be important for proper worm locomotion.
source: Here, clec-41, a gene previously found to be important for proper worm locomotion (Simmer et al., 2003), was found to be expressed and edited within the 3' untranslated region (UTR) in neural cells.
evidence: This is cited from the Simmer et al. study.

claim: Transgenic worms express higher levels of clec-41 in neural cells compared to wild-type worms.
source: Compared to wild-type worms, both transgenic lines express higher levels of clec-41 in neural cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 5A.

claim: adr-2(-) worms exhibit reduced chemotaxis indices to both benzaldehyde and trimethylthiazole compared to wild-type worms.
source: Similar to previous results obtained using a different deletion allele of adr-2, worms lacking adr-2(-) (adr-2(ok735)) exhibited reduced chemotaxis indices to both benzaldehyde and trimethylthiazole compared to wild-type worms (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is experimental data from chemotaxis assays shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Expression of clec-41 within the neural cells of adr-2(-) worms led to a significant increase in the chemotaxis indices.
source: Strikingly, expression of clec-41 within the neural cells of adr-2(-) worms led to a significant increase in the chemotaxis indices (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is experimental data from chemotaxis assays shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The increased expression of clec-41 within neural cells did not significantly increase the chemotaxis index over wild-type worms.
source: Importantly, the increased expression of clec-41 within neural cells did not significantly increase the chemotaxis index over wild-type worms.
evidence: This is a statistical observation from the chemotaxis data.

claim: Expression of the clec-41 3' UTR in neural cells was not sufficient to restore chemotaxis to adr-2(-) worms.
source: In addition, expression of the clec-41 3' UTR in neural cells was not sufficient to restore chemotaxis to adr-2(-) worms nor was expression of clec-41 in nonneural tissue (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is experimental data from chemotaxis assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of clec-41 in nonneural tissue was not sufficient to restore chemotaxis to adr-2(-) worms.
source: In addition, expression of the clec-41 3' UTR in neural cells was not sufficient to restore chemotaxis to adr-2(-) worms nor was expression of clec-41 in nonneural tissue (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is experimental data from chemotaxis assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Restoring CLEC-41 expression within neural cells is sufficient to prevent disruptions in chemotaxis specifically associated with loss of adr-2.
source: This data suggests restoring CLEC-41 expression within neural cells is sufficient to prevent disruptions in chemotaxis specifically associated with loss of adr-2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: The adr-2(gk777511) strain has a single nucleotide mutation that results in the incorporation of an arginine instead of a conserved glycine at amino acid 184 (G184R).
source: The adr-2(gk777511) strain has a single nucleotide mutation that results in the incorporation of an arginine instead of a conserved glycine at amino acid 184 (G184R) and will hereafter be referred to as the adr-2(G184R) worms (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is information about the mutant strain shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At all 40 adenosines edited in wild-type worms, editing was absent in adr-2(G184R) worms.
source: At all 40 adenosines edited in wild-type worms, editing was absent in adr-2(G184R) worms, similar to worms lacking adr-2 (Figure 6B, data not shown).
evidence: This is experimental data from Sanger sequencing shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Similar levels of ADR-2 protein were immunoprecipitated from both wild-type and adr-2(G184R) worms.
source: Using a custom antibody that is specific for ADR-2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), similar levels of ADR-2 protein were immunoprecipitated from both wild-type and adr-2(G184R) worms, whereas no ADR-2 protein was immunoprecipitated from the adr-2(-) worms (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is experimental data from immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 6C.

claim: No ADR-2 protein was immunoprecipitated from the adr-2(-) worms.
source: Using a custom antibody that is specific for ADR-2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), similar levels of ADR-2 protein were immunoprecipitated from both wild-type and adr-2(G184R) worms, whereas no ADR-2 protein was immunoprecipitated from the adr-2(-) worms (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is experimental data from immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 6C.

claim: clec-41 mRNA shows >20 fold enrichment in immunoprecipitations from both wild-type and adr-2(G184R) worms compared to those lacking adr-2.
